title: Midnight.
paragraphs: Midnight.

No trumpet.
No thunder.
No army marching.
Just silence…
The kind of silence that makes your chest tighten.
Because something had just happened across an entire empire.
And by morning, Egypt would never be the same.
The Bible records one of the most terrifying nights in human history.

Not myth.
Not legend.
Not poetry.
Judgment.
After nine devastating plagues, Pharaoh still refused to release the Israelites from slavery. The Nile had turned to blood. Frogs flooded the land. Darkness swallowed Egypt for three days.
Yet Pharaoh’s heart remained hard.
So God declared the final plague.

“About midnight I will go throughout Egypt. Every firstborn son in Egypt will die.”
— Exodus 11:4–5

From the palace of Pharaoh…
to the poorest house…
even the firstborn of livestock.

No rank.
No wealth.
No power.
Nothing could stop what was coming.
Except one thing.
God gave Israel an instruction that sounded strange—but it would mean the difference between life and death.
Each household had to take a perfect lamb.

Not sick.
Not weak.
Not flawed.
Perfect.
They were to sacrifice the lamb and place its blood on the doorposts and lintel of their house.
Then God spoke a sentence that echoes across the centuries:

“The blood shall be a sign for you… and when I see the blood, I will pass over you.”
— Exodus 12:13
Not when I see your good deeds.
Not when I see your religion.
Not when I see your effort.
When I see the blood.
Imagine the tension that night.
Fathers carefully brushing blood onto wooden doorposts.
Mothers holding their children inside.
Lamps flickering.
Outside…
A nation waiting in darkness.
Inside those homes, families ate the Passover meal exactly as God commanded — roasted lamb, unleavened bread, and bitter herbs (Exodus 12:8).
Shoes on their feet.
Staffs in their hands.
Ready to leave slavery behind.
Because God was about to move.
Then midnight came.
The Bible describes it with chilling clarity:

“At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt.”
— Exodus 12:29
From Pharaoh’s son who sat on the throne…
to the prisoner in the dungeon.
The plague touched every Egyptian household.
And suddenly the silence broke.

“There was a loud wailing in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead.”
— Exodus 12:30
Imagine hearing that cry echo through the streets.
Grief.
Shock.
Terror.
The entire empire awakened in mourning.
But in the houses marked with blood…
The firstborn lived.
Not because they were perfect.
Not because they were righteous.
But because the lamb had died in their place.
That very night Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron.
His pride was shattered.
His power broken.
And he finally said the words he had refused to say for months:

“Rise up, go out from among my people.”
— Exodus 12:31
After 430 years of slavery, Israel walked out of Egypt.
Chains broken.
Promises fulfilled.
But the story doesn’t end there.
Because the Passover lamb was never just about Egypt.
It was a shadow.
A prophecy.
A preview of something far greater.
More than 1,400 years later, another Lamb would appear.
When John the Baptist saw Jesus Christ, he declared:

“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.”
— John 1:29
Jesus would become the ultimate Passover Lamb.
Perfect.
Without sin.
Sacrificed not for one nation—but for the whole world.
The apostle Paul wrote:

“Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”
— 1 Corinthians 5:7
Just like in Egypt…
Judgment passes through the world.
But those covered by the blood of Christ are spared.
Not because we deserve it.
Not because we earned it.
Because Jesus took the judgment we deserved.
The tenth plague forces every reader of Scripture to face an uncomfortable truth.
God is not only loving.
He is also just.
Sin has consequences.
Rebellion has a cost.
But the same God who brought judgment also provided a way of rescue.
The blood of the lamb.
And ultimately…
The blood of Christ.
So the real question isn’t just about Egypt.
It’s about you.
If you lived in Egypt that night, you had only two choices:
Ignore the warning…
or trust the blood.
That same choice still stands today.
Because the cross of Jesus is the ultimate Passover doorpost.
And the promise still echoes across history:

“When I see the blood, I will pass over you.”
— Exodus 12:13
If this message moved you, pause for a moment.
Reflect.
Because the story of the tenth plague is not just about judgment.
It’s about salvation.
It’s about the Lamb.
And it’s about the God who still rescues people from slavery to sin.
We tell the stories that shame tried to erase.
